content: Tin pest is an autocatalytic and allotropic transformation of the element tin, which leads to the degradation of tin objects when exposed to low temperatures. This phenomenon is also referred to as tin disease or tin leprosy (Lèpre d'étain). During the medieval period in Europe, it was observed that the pipes of church pipe organs were affected in colder climates. Once the tin began to decompose, the process accelerated and appeared to perpetuate itself. At temperatures of 2 degrees Celsius (approximately 35.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and below, pure tin undergoes a transformation from its silvery, ductile β-modification (white tin) to a brittle α-modification (grey tin). Over time, this transformation results in the material disintegrating into powder, which is why it is called tin pest. The decomposition process is self-catalyzing, meaning that the presence of tin pest promotes further transformation of surrounding tin into tin pest. Consequently, tin objects exposed to low temperatures will eventually disintegrate entirely. Possible Historical Examples Scott Expedition to Antarctica In 1910, British polar explorer Robert Scott embarked on an expedition to become the first to reach the South Pole, but he was ultimately beaten by Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen. The expedition traversed the frozen Antarctic deserts on foot, relying on caches of food and kerosene that had been deposited along their route. However, in early 1912, upon reaching the first cache, they discovered that there was no kerosene. The cans, which had been soldered with tin, were found to be empty. Tragically, members of the expedition later perished in the extreme cold and blizzards, just 11 miles from a large depot of supplies. The exact cause of the empty tins remains unknown. Some have attributed it to poor-quality soldering, although tin cans over 80 years old have been found in Antarctic buildings with their soldering still intact. Regardless, the absence of kerosene was only one of several factors contributing to the deaths. One source suggests that the likely causes of death for Scott's polar party were a combination of scurvy, gangrene, starvation, dehydration, and hypothermia. Napoleon's Buttons A frequently recounted story involves Napoleon's soldiers suffering in the harsh Russian winter, with their clothing falling apart as tin pest degraded the buttons. Whether failing buttons were indeed a contributing factor to the failure of the invasion remains a matter of debate. Critics of this theory argue that the tin used at the time would have been quite impure, making it more resistant to cold temperatures. Laboratory tests have shown that unalloyed tin requires approximately 18 months of exposure to low temperatures to develop significant tin pest damage, which is more than twice the duration of Napoleon's Russian campaign. Modern Tin In contemporary applications, tin casting and plating processes are designed to avoid the occurrence of tin pest. This is achieved by alloying tin with small amounts of antimony or bismuth, which inhibit the decomposition process. Other elements, such as silver, indium, and lead, have also been used to prevent tin pest.
